question: Can a carefully chosen example break a proposed mathematical rule?
idea: A general rule says something must always happen under particular assumptions. One example satisfying those assumptions but violating the conclusion would overturn the rule. This entry reports such a construction; the exact rule and conditions are stated below.
why: The study of collections of transformations acting on spaces of functions. These structures appear in quantum theory and infinite-dimensional geometry.

glossary.meaning: A mathematical condition that rules out certain forms of escaping to infinity; in ordinary Euclidean space it means closed and bounded.
A collection of operators with algebraic and analytic structure; these objects are important in quantum mathematics.
A transformation that takes a vector or function and produces another one.
A single valid object or case that violates a proposed general statement.
A way of measuring the number of independent directions or degrees of freedom; different theories use different notions.

exactClaim: Gives an alternative to [Tanaka's ZFC construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26930v1) of a unital infinite-dimensional simple complex C∗-algebra with a faithful tracial state and exactly one nonzero irreducible representation up to unitary equivalence. Thus the unrestricted compact-operator characterization fails without additional set-theoretic assumptions; the counterexample is nonseparable.
scope: A definition-led reading guide; the exact mathematical claim is preserved separately. This is not a proof assessment.
